content.question_text: With what can you convert a primitive type into an object?

core_requirements: Wrapper classes (e.g., Integer, Double, Boolean, etc.).
acceptable_variations: Wrapper classes like Integer or Double

content.question_text: Are wrapper classes mutable or immutable?

core_requirements: No — wrapper classes are immutable.

content.question_text: Can you extend a wrapper class?

core_requirements: No — wrapper classes are final and cannot be extended.

content.question_text: How do you declare an ArrayList that stores integers?

core_requirements: ArrayList<Integer>

content.question_text: Why is an ArrayList of wrapper class Integer less efficient than a regular array of int?

core_requirements: Each int value is wrapped inside an Integer object.
This adds memory overhead due to object headers and storage of reference pointers.
acceptable_variations: Wrapper objects consume more memory than primitive values

content.question_text: For what kind of collections should ArrayLists with wrapper classes be used?

core_requirements: For smaller collections where the convenience of using wrapper classes is more important than raw performance/efficiency.
acceptable_variations: For small collections where ease of use outweighs performance concerns

core_requirements: The automatic conversion of a primitive type to its corresponding wrapper class.
Example: int to Integer automatically.
acceptable_variations: Java automatically wraps primitives when needed

core_requirements: The automatic conversion of a wrapper class object to its corresponding primitive type.
Example: Integer to int automatically.
acceptable_variations: Java automatically unwraps wrapper objects when needed

content.question_text: When comparing wrapper classes with primitive types, what is important to remember about the == operator?

core_requirements: You cannot safely use == to compare wrapper class objects for value equality.
== compares object references, not the values.
You should use the .equals() method instead to compare values.

content.question_text: What is the exception where == might work for wrapper classes?

core_requirements: For values between -128 and 127 (the Integer cache range), Java reuses wrapper objects.
== may appear to work for these values because they reference the same cached objects.
acceptable_variations: The Integer cache range -128 to 127 can make == work
Only for small values where Java caches wrapper objects

content.question_text: How should you construct a wrapper class object, and why should you avoid using constructors?

core_requirements: Use the .valueOf() method or rely on autoboxing.
Wrapper class constructors are deprecated and marked for removal in future Java versions.
acceptable_variations: Use valueOf() or autoboxing instead of new Integer()
Constructors are deprecated; use valueOf instead

content.question_text: Can unboxing throw a NullPointerException? If so, why?

core_requirements: Yes, unboxing can throw a NullPointerException.
Because a wrapper object reference can be null, and attempting to unbox a null reference into a primitive results in NullPointerException.
acceptable_variations: Yes, if the wrapper is null when unboxing

content.question_text: What other useful features do wrapper classes provide beyond wrapping primitives?

core_requirements: Wrapper classes provide useful static methods for converting strings to values (e.g., Integer.parseInt()).
They also provide constants like Integer.MAX_VALUE, Integer.MIN_VALUE, etc.
acceptable_variations: Utility methods for parsing, conversion, and constants

core_requirements: Double.MIN_VALUE is the smallest positive (non-zero) value that a double can represent.
It is not the most negative value (that would be -Double.MAX_VALUE).
